The trade in brazilwood, a tree of Brazil's Atlantic forest whose red heartwood gave a valuable dye, was the first business of Portuguese Brazil. Europe already used a red dye wood from Asia called "brasil", from a word for ember. When the Portuguese found a similar tree, the land itself came to be called Brazil.

From 1501 the Portuguese crown leased the trade to merchants, among them the Lisbon trader Fernão de Loronha. They set up small posts on the coast. The Tupi peoples cut the heavy logs and carried them to the ships in exchange for metal tools, cloth and trinkets. French traders soon competed along the same coast.

The dye coloured cloth across Europe. By the 1530s the crown was granting land to settlers, and sugar grown with enslaved labour replaced brazilwood as the colony's main export. Overcutting nearly wiped out the tree. Today its hard wood is still prized for violin bows, and it is Brazil's national tree.
